strengths: Well-motivated alternative to diffusion paradigm with genuine practical advantages (completion, outpainting) naturally supported by autoregressive formulation
Strong quantitative results on object generation (chairs): best FID, KID, and COV compared to L3DG, DiffRF, and other methods
Thoughtful architectural design with separate position/feature vocabularies, 3D RoPE with token-type dimension, and effective geometry-appearance decoupling
Comprehensive implementation details and extensive appendix supporting reproducibility (hyperparameters, loss definitions, initialization schemes)
Demonstrates versatility: single model handles unconditional generation, completion, and large-scale outpainting through natural prefix conditioning
Ablation study on serialization strategies provides useful insights into ordering effects independent of spatial priors
weaknesses: Critical gap: scene generation only qualitatively compared to L3DG without quantitative metrics (FID, KID, MMD); claims about scene generation advantages lack rigorous evidence
Computational efficiency not competitive: 12m × 12m scene generation takes ~1.67 hours on GH200 GPU; no wall-clock comparison with diffusion baselines to justify cost-benefit tradeoff
Real-world applicability under-developed: ScanNet++ results relegated to appendix with acknowledged autoencoder fidelity limitations; only 895 scenes and acknowledged noisiness issues
Limited technical novelty: components largely from prior work (sparse 3D CNN from L3DG, LFQ, 3D RoPE); contribution is primarily in combination rather than fundamental innovation
Incomplete technical justifications: why xyz ordering sufficient without 3D locality? No ablations on 3D RoPE vs. 1D encoding, separate vocabularies, or chunking strategy
Spatial coherence analysis absent: no quantitative metrics for long-range consistency, wall continuity across chunks, or physical plausibility of generated layouts
Chunking strategy adds complexity with design choices (size, overlap, context positioning) and resampling heuristic (up to 5 retries) without clear justification or analysis of quality impact
Limited scope: focus on synthetic indoor scenes; generalization to other domains, real-world imperfections, and diverse scene types unclear

strengths: Well-motivated autoregressive approach with clear advantages for scene completion and outpainting tasks; naturally supports incremental construction paradigm
Strong quantitative results on shape synthesis (SOTA on PhotoShape: FID 5.68 vs L3DG 8.49) with cleaner Gaussian allocations
Thoughtfully designed technical components: separate position/feature vocabularies, 3D RoPE for spatial awareness, LFQ for better codebook utilization
Comprehensive experimental coverage: ablations on serialization strategies, real-world validation on ScanNet++, extensive implementation details and reproducibility information
Excellent presentation: clear methodology, detailed configurations, thorough appendix, well-organized writing
Flexible inference capabilities naturally supported: temperature-based sampling, tree search for connectivity, masking for constraints
weaknesses: Scene generation results lack quantitative evaluation; comparison to L3DG and other baselines is primarily visual/qualitative, making it impossible to assess whether scenes are actually superior to diffusion methods
Significant degradation on real-world data (ScanNet++): visible artifacts, noisy geometry, acknowledged autoencoder reconstruction fidelity bottleneck limits practical applicability
Slow inference for large scenes (~1.67 hours for 12m×12m on GH200 GPU); requires multiple resampling attempts; no timing comparison to diffusion or other baselines provided
Limited baseline comparisons for scene generation: only L3DG compared; no comparisons to DiffuScene, SceneFormer, or other recent scene generation methods
Claimed advantages over diffusion (compositionality, diversity, single-pass generation) not quantitatively validated; iterative outpainting partially undermines single-pass claim
Sequence ordering ablation lacks depth: explanation relies on '3D RoPE compensates' without theoretical justification; no analysis of what patterns different orderings capture
Scope limited to structured indoor scenes with regular layouts; generalization to outdoor/unstructured environments unclear; real-world domain gap is substantial
Missing quantitative metrics for scenes: no FID/KID, diversity measures, or scene-specific quality metrics; unclear if this is engineering limitation or fundamental disadvantage
Chunking introduces design choices (overlap strategy, window positioning) requiring careful tuning; boundary effects across chunks not systematically analyzed
Insufficient ablations: no study of chunk size effects, transformer architecture choices, vocabulary size sensitivity, or failure mode analysis

strengths: Novel perspective on 3D scene generation through token-based autoregressive modeling with explicit spatial structure preservation
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple tasks (unconditional generation, scene completion, large-scale synthesis) and datasets
Strong quantitative results on synthetic data with competitive/superior metrics to baselines on multiple measures (FID, appearance quality, layout)
Thoughtful technical design with well-motivated components: sparse 3D encoding, vector quantization, 3D rotary positional embeddings, separate vocabularies for decoupling geometry and appearance
Detailed ablation studies (Tables 3-4) justifying design choices and demonstrating the contribution of individual components
Demonstrated scalability to 12m×12m scenes beyond training horizons with analysis of quality degradation patterns
Well-written paper with clear presentation, informative figures, and practical engineering solutions documented in appendices
weaknesses: Significant computational efficiency disadvantage: 3.3× slower inference (78.1s vs 23.8s) and 3.2× higher memory consumption (5.04 GB vs 1.55 GB) compared to L3DG baseline, severely limiting practical applicability without proposed optimizations

Limited novelty in individual components: 3D Gaussian Splatting, vector-quantized autoencoders, and 3D rotary embeddings are existing techniques; primary contribution is engineering and combination rather than algorithmic innovation

Substantial real-world performance degradation on ScanNet++ (Appendix A) with limited analysis: autoencoder fidelity acknowledged as limiting but implications for deployment underexplored; training on only 895 real scenes versus 25,000 synthetic

Incomplete experimental comparisons: scene generation benchmarked against only L3DG; missing comparisons with other recent methods (ATISS, LayoutGPT, DreamScene) mentioned in related work; no user studies for perceptual validation

Unresolved quality-diversity trade-off: GaussianGPT achieves lower geometry metrics than L3DG in scene completion (84.14 vs 83.84 MMD in generation; 90.77 vs 111.71 in 50% context) with more varied completions from L3DG; paper lacks clear guidance on method selection

Limited theoretical justification for design choices: why autoregressive token generation is appropriate for geometric structure, z-order traversal superiority over alternatives, and the causal connection between sequential generation and spatial coherence not rigorously established

Incomplete ablation studies: no empirical comparison of serialization alternatives, quantified comparison of 3D RoPE versus standard positional encodings, transformer architecture sensitivity, or individual loss component contributions

Scalability limitations inadequately discussed: quality degrades with distance from initial context (Fig. 9), requires resampling/backtracking strategies, fixed training chunk size constraints, and applicability to large unbounded real-world scenes unclear
